# Democracy experiment {#sec-gs}

@graham2020democracy ask whether voters punish candidates who violate democratic principles when
party and policy favor them. In their experiment, each respondent chose sixteen times between two
hypothetical state legislative candidates who varied in party, economic and social policy,
governance practices, democratic violations, scandals, and personal traits, and the analysis keeps
up to thirteen of these choices. This chapter reproduces the paper's results from the saved fit.

```{r}
#| label: gs-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
gs <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
if (is.null(gs)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit gs_q3.rds; see the installation chapter.")
# a short table of estimates
tab <- function(e, digits = 3) {
  out <- e[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "se", "lower", "upper", "n")]
  out[2:6] <- lapply(out[2:6], round, digits)
  out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: gs-knitr
#| include: false
#| cache: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(pointsize = 11))
```

The chunk below loads two helpers from the book's `_figs-helpers.R`: `estimate_each()` runs
independent targets in parallel with the same results as one `sc_estimate()` call, while `pick()`
selects rows by name. The figures come from the package's plot functions (@sec-plots).

```{r}
#| label: gs-helpers
#| cache: false
#| file: _figs-helpers.R
```

## Data and fit

Calling `sc_example_data("gs")` constructs the paper's inputs from the bundled `gs2020` data,
covering 1,605 respondents, 20,657 matchups, and 30 coded features, with `y = 1` indicating that
the left candidate was chosen. Alongside the choices and features, the object holds the sixteen
respondent characteristics measured before the tasks that enter the network, the paper's five folds
together with each fold's validation respondents (used to stop training early), and the grouping
variables.

```{r}
#| label: gs-data
x <- sc_example_data("gs")
x
head(x$groups)
```

The grouping variables are party ID (`pid7`, running from -3 for strong Democrat to 3 for strong
Republican), party (`party`, with leaners counted as partisans), self-described ideology
(`ideology`, covering all respondents), and an indicator (`PL`) equal to 1 for the 1,377 partisans
and leaners. For the remaining 228 pure independents, the co-partisan feature is always zero and
their choices say nothing about that taste, so quantities about party use `w = "PL"`.

To select the number of taste factors, the paper fitted models with one to four factors and chose
three. Because the defaults of `sc_fit()` and `sc_states()` match the paper's settings, the code
below reproduces the saved fit; it takes several hours to run and is therefore not evaluated here.

```{r}
#| label: gs-fit
#| eval: false
fit_q <- lapply(1:4, function(q) sc_fit(x, q = q))   # five folds at each rank
sc_select_rank(fit_q)
gs <- sc_states(fit_q[[3]])                           # q = 3; M = 300 designs, 4 responses each
sc_save(gs, file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
```

Each candidate rank is evaluated by its held-out log score, defined as the average log probability
of a held-out respondent's whole sequence of choices. Calling `sc_select_rank()` gives the paper's
rank table:

| Taste factors | Held-out log score | Gain over $q - 1$ | Paired $z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | -7.797 | | |
| 2 | -7.772 | 0.0249 | 2.19 |
| 3 (selected) | -7.739 | 0.0329 | 2.99 |
| 4 | -7.742 | -0.0029 | -0.47 |

Because adding a fourth factor does not improve the held-out log score, the rule stops at $q = 3$.

## Mean tastes

To estimate the average utility of a single coded feature on the logit scale, the package provides
`sc_mean()`. Following the grouping convention above, the co-partisan mean averages over partisans
and leaners while all other feature means average over all respondents.

```{r}
#| label: gs-means
fn <- gs$data$data$feature_names
w_of <- function(f) if (f == "diff_respParty") "PL" else NULL
means <- sc_estimate(gs, lapply(fn, function(f) sc_mean(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
labels <- c("Co-partisan", "Economic policy (+1)", "Social policy (+1)",
            "Committee structure", "Legislative staffing", "Legislative procedure",
            "Program evaluation", "Record-keeping", "Legislative schedule",
            "Ban protests", "Ignore courts", "Executive orders", "Gerrymander (2 seats)",
            "Gerrymander (10 seats)", "Prosecute journalists", "Close polling stations",
            "Extramarital affair", "Underpaid taxes", "Female", "Asian", "Black", "Hispanic",
            "Farmer", "Lawyer", "Legislative staffer", "Police officer", "Army veteran",
            "Navy veteran", "Small business owner", "Teacher")
tab(means[c(1:3, 10:18), ])
```

Among partisans and leaners, a co-partisan gains 0.81 units of utility on average, while each step
toward the conservative end of economic policy costs 0.24. Conduct is measured against the generic
reference position --- a candidate who supports an elected oversight board: the seven violations
(`u_`) have mean utilities running from -0.53 for a two-seat gerrymander to -0.90 for prosecuting
journalists, and the two scandals (`v_`) cost -0.94 for an affair and -1.18 for underpaid taxes.

In the table above, `plug_in` reports the cross-fitted value before the one-step correction
(@sec-inference).

## Preference shares

To estimate the share of respondents with a positive taste for a contrast, `sc_share()` averages
over each respondent's fitted normal law. The main figure reports these shares for party, the two
policy scales, the seven violations, and the two scandals. Each share requires a separate
refinement that keeps the estimate between 0 and 1 --- a bounded update (@sec-quantities) --- and
because each update takes about 15 seconds, they are run in parallel.

```{r}
#| label: gs-shares
fig_features <- fn[c(1:3, 10:18)]
shares <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, function(f) sc_share(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
tab(shares, 4)
```

An estimated 82.5% of partisans and leaners prefer a co-partisan (95% interval 79.7% to 84.9%). By
contrast, the shares favoring a violation are near zero and imprecise: 7.3% for closing polling
stations (interval 2.0% to 23.4%) and 0.2% for prosecuting journalists (interval 0 to 1). That
imprecision arises because such a share depends on the spread of the taste, which is itself
measured imprecisely because each respondent saw each violation once.

## Fitted distributions

For a given feature, `sc_fitted_law()` returns each held-out respondent's normal law for that taste
--- combining the fitted mean with the spread implied by the taste factors --- and the population
law is the mixture of those respondent-level laws.

```{r}
#| label: gs-laws
laws <- lapply(fn, function(f) sc_fitted_law(gs, f, w = w_of(f)))
attr(laws[[1]], "summary")
head(laws[[1]])
```

The figure below shows the fitted laws of all thirty tastes on one axis, grouped by attribute,
while the full inventory is retained in the replication materials.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Fitted tastes, by attribute"
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 13
attribute <- c("Party", rep("Policy", 2), rep("Governance", 6), rep("Violations", 7),
               rep("Scandals", 2), "Sex", rep("Race", 3), rep("Profession", 8))
sc_plot_laws(laws, labels = labels, means = pick(means, fn), groups = attribute, height = 1.3,
             bins = 300, outline = "line", xlim = c(-4, 4), xlab = "Taste (logit units)")
```

Each curve shows fitted values before the one-step correction, and its vertical line marks the
corrected mean, so the two need not line up. All thirty tastes share one axis, and the reference
levels are male, white, and business executive.

## Effects on choices

The model's counterpart to the AMCE is the average marginal effect (AME) of switching one attribute
of a candidate, which `sc_ame_switch()` computes from the raw design attribute, the level, and the
reference level (@sec-quantities). For party, the level is the respondent's own party (1 =
Democrat, 2 = Republican) and the reference is the other party, leaving the switch undefined for
pure independents. A policy AME switches from position 1 to 4 and divides by three to give the
effect per point, while a conduct AME switches from the generic reference position (`g_boardElect`)
to the violation.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ames
ame_target <- function(f) {
  if (f == "diff_respParty") {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "party",
                  level = function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  ref = function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  design = "gs", w = "PL")
  } else if (f %in% c("diff_p1_num", "diff_p2_num")) {
    sc_ame_switch(f, sub("^diff_(p[12])_num$", "\\1", f), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3)
  } else {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "dem", f, "g_boardElect", design = "gs")
  }
}
ames <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, ame_target))
tab(ames)
```

For comparison, the regression AMCEs are the coefficients of a linear regression of the choice on
all 30 coded differences, fitted among all respondents (among partisans and leaners for party).

```{r}
#| label: gs-amce
dat <- gs$data$data                                    # y: choices; d: coded differences
partisan_rows <- rep(gs$data$groups$PL, dat$T) > 0
amce_all <- coef(lm(dat$y ~ dat$d))[-1]
amce_pl <- coef(lm(dat$y[partisan_rows] ~ dat$d[partisan_rows, ]))[-1]
amce <- setNames(c(amce_pl[1], amce_all[-1]), fn)
round(100 * amce[fig_features], 1)
```

Under the model, a co-partisan gains 14.0 percentage points of support and a candidate who
prosecutes journalists loses 16.2, compared with regression AMCEs of 14.1 and -16.1.

The main figure brings these summaries together: each feature's mean taste (A), its fitted
distribution (B), the share with a positive taste (C), and its AME alongside the regression AMCE as
a grey diamond (D).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-preferences
#| fig-cap: "Preferences and choice effects"
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 5.5
lab <- setNames(labels, fn)
sc_plot_preferences(means, setNames(laws, fn), shares, ames, labels = lab, reference = amce,
                    order = fig_features, groups = setNames(attribute, fn)[fig_features],
                    xlim = list(A = c(-1.55, 1.2), B = c(-4.6, 4.6), C = c(-6, 106), D = c(-26, 18)),
                    # ticks off the panels' edges, so neighbouring labels do not touch
                    ticks = list(A = c(-1, 0, 1), B = c(-4, 0, 4), D = c(-20, 0, 15)))
```

Because Panel B's curves show fitted values before the one-step correction and are scaled to the
same height, their centers need not match Panel A. In Panel C, a hollow point marks a share whose
interval spans at least 95 points, and that interval is not drawn.

The same estimates can be formatted as a table with `sc_table()` (@sec-plots):

```{r}
#| label: gs-table
#| results: asis
sc_table("Mean utility" = means, "Share favoring" = shares, "Choice effect" = ames,
         order = fig_features, labels = lab, format = "markdown", n = TRUE)
```

## Compensation shares

The share of respondents who prefer a co-partisan with a violation to an otherwise identical
non-co-partisan at the generic reference position is the *compensation share*. In `sc_share()`,
this contrast is the sum of the two features. The paper computes it for the seven violations among
liberal, moderate, and conservative partisans and leaners, which requires 21 bounded updates.

```{r}
#| label: gs-comp
g <- gs$data$groups
violations <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn, value = TRUE)
comp <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (f in violations)
  comp[[length(comp) + 1]] <- sc_share(paste(ideo, f, sep = "."), c(f, "diff_respParty"),
                                       w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
comp_est <- estimate_each(gs, comp)
tab(comp_est[grepl("journalists", comp_est$name), ])
```

Even with its large mean penalty, an estimated 33.8% of liberal partisans and leaners and 59.6% of
conservative ones prefer the co-partisan who prosecutes journalists.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-compensation
#| fig-cap: "Compensation shares"
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
by_ideology <- function(ideo) {       # one group's rows, named by violation
  z <- pick(comp_est, paste(ideo, violations, sep = ".")); z$name <- violations; z
}
sc_plot_estimates(Liberal = by_ideology("lib"), Moderate = by_ideology("mod"),
                  Conservative = by_ideology("con"), labels = lab, scale = 100, xlim = c(0, 100),
                  xlab = "Share preferring co-partisan despite violation (%)",
                  main = "Party advantage offsets the violation")
```

In the figure, points show bounded estimates and bars show 95% log-odds intervals.

To express the mean prosecution penalty in units of the mean partisan gain, `sc_ratio()` returns
$-\tau_j / \tau_p$ with a delta-method standard error, where $\tau_j$ is the mean taste for
prosecuting journalists and $\tau_p$ is the mean co-partisan taste.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ratio
price <- sc_ratio("journalists penalty / co-partisan gain",
                  sc_mean("journalists, partisans", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", w = "PL"),
                  sc_mean("co-partisan", "diff_respParty", w = "PL"))
tab(sc_estimate(gs, price))
```

The estimated ratio is 1.14 (95% interval 0.91 to 1.37), indicating that on average the two are of
similar size.

## Candidate contests

To estimate the expected share choosing the first candidate in a specified matchup, `sc_contest()`
takes the coded difference between the two candidates as its contrast, sets position effects to
zero, and keeps task shocks (the logistic noise in each choice). Following the paper, the code
below places a co-partisan --- either with a clean record or prosecuting journalists --- at each
social-policy position (1 most liberal, 4 most conservative) against a non-co-partisan at position
3, all else equal, among liberal, moderate, and conservative partisans and leaners.

```{r}
#| label: gs-contests
e <- function(f) as.numeric(fn %in% f)
contests <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
  d <- e("diff_respParty") + (pos - 3) * e("diff_p2_num")
  if (violation == "journalists") d <- d + e("diff_dem_code_u_journalists")
  contests[[length(contests) + 1]] <- sc_contest(paste(ideo, violation, pos, sep = "."), d,
                                                 w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
}
contest_est <- sc_estimate(gs, contests)
wide <- matrix(round(100 * contest_est$estimate, 1), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(paste(rep(c("liberal", "moderate", "conservative"), each = 2),
                                     c("clean", "journalists"), sep = ", "),
                               paste("position", 1:4)))
wide
```

At position 2, the co-partisan who prosecutes journalists receives an estimated 49.8% among liberal
partisans and leaners and 52.1% among conservative ones, compared with 74.2% and 67.7% without the
violation --- a cost of about 24 and 16 points. Because these vote shares include task shocks,
they differ from the compensation shares.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-contests
#| fig-cap: "Expected support in candidate contests"
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.3
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4), 2, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(3, .35))
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) {
  row <- function(v) pick(contest_est, paste(ideo, v, 1:4, sep = "."))
  sc_plot_lines("No violation" = row("clean"), "Prosecutes journalists" = row("journalists"),
                x = 1:4, scale = 100, xlab = "Social policy position",
                ylab = if (ideo == "lib") "Expected vote share (%)" else "",
                main = c(lib = "Liberal", mod = "Moderate", con = "Conservative")[[ideo]], legend = FALSE)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("No violation", "Prosecutes journalists"), col = c(blue, red), lty = 1:2,
       lwd = 1.5, pch = 16, pt.cex = .7, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, cex = .85)
```

Shading gives pointwise 95% log-odds intervals.

## Attribute importance

To measure each attribute's share of a respondent's utility variation over a stated menu of levels,
`sc_importance()` is called on seven attributes from the paper: party, the two four-point policy
scales, the fifteen governance, violation, and scandal codes grouped as one attribute, sex, race,
and profession. Because a policy scale has a single column, its menu is specified as `matrix(1:4)`.
The shares are evaluated separately for all partisans and leaners, Democrats, and Republicans
(leaners included).

Within each group, the shares sum to one and come from one joint bounded update taking about nine
minutes per group. No intervals are reported because in the paper's simulations such intervals
cover less often than stated.

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance
attrs <- list(party = "diff_respParty", econ = "diff_p1_num", social = "diff_p2_num",
              conduct = grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn, value = TRUE),
              sex = grep("^diff_sex_", fn, value = TRUE),
              race = grep("^diff_race_", fn, value = TRUE),
              profession = grep("^diff_pro_", fn, value = TRUE))
imp_groups <- list(All = "PL", Dem = function(g) g$party == "Dem", Rep = function(g) g$party == "Rep")
imp <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sc_importance(attrs, menus = list(econ = matrix(1:4), social = matrix(1:4)),
                w = imp_groups[[k]], names = paste(k, names(attrs), sep = "."))))
imp[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "n", "status")]
```

For display, the figure groups the components into four categories: policy (economic and social),
party, governance and conduct, and background (sex, race, and profession).

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance-summary
combine <- list(policy = c("econ", "social"), party = "party", governance = "conduct",
                background = c("sex", "race", "profession"))
imp_display <- sapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sapply(combine, function(a) sum(pick(imp, paste(k, a, sep = "."))$estimate)))
round(100 * imp_display, 1)
```

Among all partisans and leaners, policy accounts for 46.5% of utility variation, followed by party
at 32.9%, governance and conduct at 18.3%, and background at 2.3%. By party, policy outweighs party
among Democrats (52.5% against 29.5%), whereas the two are close among Republicans (39.7% against
36.7%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-importance
#| fig-cap: "Attribute importance by party"
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
sc_plot_importance("All partisans and leaners" = imp[startsWith(imp$name, "All."), ],
                   Democrat = imp[startsWith(imp$name, "Dem."), ],
                   Republican = imp[startsWith(imp$name, "Rep."), ],
                   combine = combine, colors = c("#333333", blue, red),
                   labels = c(policy = "Policy", party = "Party", governance = "Governance/conduct",
                              background = "Background"))
```

The party subgroups contain 723 Democrats and 654 Republicans; the plotted shares are point
estimates computed with equal weights over each attribute's stated levels, summing to 100% within
each group.

## Decisiveness

To measure how often exchanging two candidates' levels on one attribute would reverse the choice
--- holding the other attributes and the task shock fixed --- `sc_decisiveness()` averages over the
matchups each respondent saw. In the call below, the conduct swaps take about twenty minutes.

```{r}
#| label: gs-decisiveness
conduct <- grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn)
action <- grep("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", fn[conduct])
generic <- c(TRUE, grepl("^diff_dem_code_g_", fn[conduct]))   # reference row plus generic codes
dec <- estimate_each(gs, list(
  sc_decisiveness(list(party = "diff_respParty"), pairs = list(party = c(2L, 1L)),
                  names = "party", w = "PL"),
  sc_decisiveness(list(conduct = fn[conduct]), pairs = list(conduct = cbind(1L + action, 1L)),
                  allowed = list(conduct = generic),
                  names = sub("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", "", fn[conduct][action]))))
tab(dec)
```

Among partisans and leaners, exchanging party reverses an estimated 36.1% of choices (95% interval
33.8% to 38.4%). By comparison, exchanging a candidate who prosecutes journalists with one at the
generic reference position reverses 32.0% (27.3% to 37.1%), the highest share among the seven
violations.

## All paper targets

The function `gs_targets()` below assembles every GS quantity in the paper's main results file: a
mean and a share for each of the 30 features, the compensation shares for seven violations in three
ideology groups, 24 contests, the switch AMEs, and the ratio. Running
`sc_estimate(gs, gs_targets(gs))` reproduces the paper's estimates, standard errors, and intervals
in about 40 minutes in one process, with most of the time spent on the bounded updates for its 51
shares.

```{r}
#| label: gs-full
gs_targets <- function(st) {
  fn <- st$data$data$feature_names; g <- st$data$groups
  e1 <- function(j) as.numeric(seq_along(fn) == j)
  tl <- list(); add <- function(t) tl[[length(tl) + 1L]] <<- t
  for (j in seq_along(fn)) {
    w <- if (j == 1L) "PL" else NULL
    add(sc_mean(paste0(fn[j], ".mean"), fn[j], w)); add(sc_share(paste0(fn[j], ".share"), fn[j], w))
  }
  actions <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn)
  for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) {
    wi <- as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL
    for (j in actions) add(sc_share(paste0("comp.", ideo, ".", fn[j]), c(fn[j], fn[1L]), wi))
    for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
      v <- e1(1L) + (pos - 3) * e1(3L)
      if (violation == "journalists") v <- v + e1(match("diff_dem_code_u_journalists", fn))
      add(sc_contest(paste0("contest.", ideo, ".", violation, ".", pos), v, w = wi))
    }
  }
  jm <- sc_mean("journalists.partisan.mean", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", "PL"); add(jm)
  for (j in c(1:3, actions, grep("^diff_dem_code_v_", fn))) {
    if (j == 1L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "party", function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                        function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]], design = "gs", w = "PL"))
    } else if (j <= 3L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), paste0("p", j - 1L), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3))
    } else {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "dem", fn[j], "g_boardElect", design = "gs"))
    }
  }
  add(sc_ratio("journalists.party.price", jm, sc_mean("diff_respParty.mean", "diff_respParty", "PL")))
  tl
}
```

As above, the policy AMEs are expressed per point of the scale.
